note: Existing-source public educational gallery: CC photos and explicitly credited Bob Harms science/education-only photographs are distinguished. Source labels and arrows are not independent specimen voucher certification.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — FOLLOW ONE TURKEY-FOOT STEM
tiles.details: Photograph the complete junction, not neighboring culms crossing in a prairie scene. Source images in panels 1 and 8 illustrate terminal branching and awned racemes but neither is a vouchered rooted Hays plant. Big bluestem is a robust perennial; head shape is a first clue, not a final determination.
tiles.short: Trace 2–6(10) relatively stout exposed terminal racemes back to ONE culm; often three, never a required count.
tiles.status: REAL FLOWERING-HEAD PHOTOS — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO SAME ROOTED LOCAL CULM

tiles.heading: 02 · OPEN THE COLLAR — TRUE LIGULE, NOT SHEATH COLOR
tiles.details: Panels 4–6 contain actual source-labeled ligule/sheath views. Open the inner blade–sheath junction and measure the free membrane with a 1-mm bar on a single identified flowering stem. Florida paspalum may also have a brown or jagged membranous ligule; compare INNER sheath (often bronze in big, greener in Florida) and lower blade taper only with matched living material. Do not make a species ID from pigment alone.
tiles.short: Membranous ligule about 0.4–2.5 mm; collar hairs may surround it but are separate structures.
tiles.status: TRUE LIGULE PHOTO PRESENT — SAME-PLANT MEASUREMENT AND FLORIDA PAIR MISSING

tiles.heading: 03 · PAIRED SPIKELETS — SESSILE AND PEDICELLED
tiles.details: On one attached flowering branch locate the sessile fertile unit and its stalked companion. The companion is NOT automatically a tiny vestige: it is often a substantial pollen-bearing spikelet in big bluestem. Panels 2–3 and 9–11 show genuine reproductive source material, but no image proves a complete matched living Hays plant and dissection. Count and measure intact pairs with a millimeter scale.
tiles.short: Sessile spikelet about 5–11 mm; pedicelled companion often well developed, staminate, about 3.5–12 mm.
tiles.status: SOURCE ANATOMY PHOTOS — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO SAME-VOUCHER ATTACHED PAIR

tiles.heading: 04 · GLUMES, LEMMA AND BENT AWN — DO NOT SWAP LABELS
tiles.details: A typical fertile sessile spikelet contains a lower sterile floret and an upper fertile floret. The glumes are NOT the awn-bearing fertile lemma: isolate each on the SAME tagged mature pair before placing arrows. Go Botany records two glumes per spikelet and glumes up to ~11 mm; a regional Missouri description gives lemma body ~5–9 mm, but do not substitute those published ranges for measurements of these photos. Kew treats the awn as arising from the notch/sinus of a two-lobed fertile lemma. Panels 3, 9 and 10 are teaching references, not independently verified organ-level arrow coordinates.
tiles.short: Two glumes enclose the sessile unit; the upper fertile lemma carries a twisted, bent awn commonly about 8–25 mm.
tiles.status: PUBLISHED MEASUREMENTS — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO DISSECTED SAME-PAIR GLUMES/LEMMA/AWN

tiles.heading: 05 · LOCAL LOOK-ALIKES — BIG, LITTLE, KR AND FLORIDA
tiles.details: Panels 12–15 show DIFFERENT species, not big bluestem. KR bluestem is introduced and can overlap in raceme count, so compare the true collar and mature spikelet pairs before management decisions. Florida paspalum is a native vegetative look-alike; its greener inner sheath and less-tapered blade base are supporting tendencies, not absolute diagnostic rules. Bushy bluestem and broomsedge have more sheathed, fluffy flowering architecture. If evidence conflicts, record bluestem sp. or Andropogoneae rather than remove a presumed invasive.
tiles.short: Big has stout terminal fingers; little has many short upper axillary racemes; KR has finer clustered terminal fingers; Indiangrass has one branched plume.
tiles.status: EXISTING LOOK-ALIKE PANELS — SAME-ANGLE FIELD COMPARISON PENDING

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE — TWO PRECISE HANDOFFS
tiles.details: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO (Grass Photo-Finish): one voucher-linked rooted Hays-area flowering culm with intact 2–6(10)-raceme terminal junction; the SAME plant's true ligule with 1-mm ruler; a mature attached sessile/pedicelled pair with separated glumes, ~5–9 mm fertile lemma and actual awn insertion at 10–20×; paired fresh split inner sheaths of big bluestem and Florida paspalum. NEEDS_SITE_QA (Public Learner Readiness): verify all ten archived image files, 15 teaching panels, authors and image-level rights (especially five Bob Harms educational-only NOT-CC originals), existing arrows against pixels, other-species labels, six-tile mobile rendering, and rights-filtered public page. No new photos, arrows or Pages publication in this run. Preserve all county/taxonomy holds and remain FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS until anatomical, license and display checks pass.
tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS: 10 existing species image records and 15 teaching panels, but decisive connected anatomy and rights/site QA remain open.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: BIG BLUESTEM: a few (often 2–6) relatively STOUT, exposed terminal turkey-foot racemes that can be traced to ONE flowering culm. For detailed identification, the learner now shows Bob Harms's actual Central Texas measured flowering-unit/spikelet and sheath images alongside two Matt Lavin membranous-ligule photos. Study REAL awned fertile sessile and pedicelled companion grass flowers, rachis hairs and their disarticulation—but don't call the tiny individual organ arrows resolved until a same-specimen attachment is inspected. Florida paspalum, also native, can mimic sterile big: big often has a bronze INNER SHEATH and a blade narrowing near collar; Florida tends GREEN inner sheath and more uniform blade width, while BOTH may have BROWN or jagged MEMBRANOUS LIGULES. These supporting differences need two opened live sheaths in matching photographs. KR is introduced, little bluestem and Indiangrass native; full branch origin beats color or 3-finger-only guesses.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: START WITH THE REAL TEXAS HEAD (photo 4): trace the flowering stem into separate terminal racemes. This is not a rooted whole plant, and 'turkey foot' shape varies.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Panels 4–6 contain actual source-labeled ligule/sheath views. Open the inner blade–sheath junction and measure the free membrane with a 1-mm bar on a single identified flowering stem. Florida paspalum may also have a brown or jagged membranous ligule; compare INNER sheath (often bronze in big, greener in Florida) and lower blade taper only with matched living material. Do not make a species ID from pigment alone.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: On one attached flowering branch locate the sessile fertile unit and its stalked companion. The companion is NOT automatically a tiny vestige: it is often a substantial pollen-bearing spikelet in big bluestem. Panels 2–3 and 9–11 show genuine reproductive source material, but no image proves a complete matched living Hays plant and dissection. Count and measure intact pairs with a millimeter scale.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Big bluestem: usually 2–6 exposed relatively stout racemes close together at the terminal head (often a turkey-foot). Little bluestem: many short silky racemes repeated on separate leafy upper branchlets. KR bluestem: long thin clustered terminal racemes, often overlapping in count, so use several characters rather than seedhead count alone. Bushy bluestem: bulky fuzzy plume. Broomsedge: narrower silky flowering units subtended by spathe-like sheaths. Indiangrass: elongated single plume-like inflorescence.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: NEW · TEXAS SOURCE — flowering culms and branching turkey-foot heads — PROVISIONAL USER REVIEW
panels.caption: Photographer-identified big bluestem photographed by the Pedernales River. Follow a single terminal head where its stout, spikelet-bearing racemes diverge near the stem tip; the arrow marks one genuine flowering raceme, NOT a rhizome or individual glume. Surrounding flowering stalks overlap, and neither entire rooted basal plant nor same-plant collar is visible.
panels.creator: Matt Lavin
panels.modifications: No edits or embedded arrows; linked original

panels.label: True big bluestem collar and membranous ligule
panels.caption: Matt Lavin's true opened Andropogon gerardi collar: the pale triangular-torn tissue at the sheath rim is a MEMBRANOUS ligule, distinct from the longer fine hairs to its right. Both arrows were re-centered onto visible photo pixels 2026-10-26; this photo shows no rooted crown, whole plant or measured length.
panels.creator: Matt Lavin

markers.label: Fine hairs beside ligule (not the membrane)

panels.label: NEW · REPRODUCTIVE PHOTO — yellow anthers on big bluestem — PROVISIONAL USER REVIEW
panels.caption: These yellow dangling structures are pollen-producing anthers. Their presence confirms the photo was taken in active flowering; the photograph does not distinguish a particular fertile lemma, its awn origin, or a paired pedicellate spikelet under 1-mm scale.
panels.creator: Matt Lavin
panels.modifications: No edits or embedded arrows; linked original
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: NO FLOWERS? Florida paspalum (DIFFERENT species): flowering habit comparison
panels.caption: PHOTO: Florida paspalum, NOT big bluestem. This licensed full-plant flowering image shows a different grass with stalks and leaves. At the blade/sheath junction use a fresh specimen: USGS notes big-bluestem blades narrow slightly near the collar and widen along the middle, often bronze cast on the inside of the sheath; Florida paspalum blades tend to maintain a steadier width and the inner sheath is typically green. THESE FINE COLOR/WIDTH FEATURES ARE NOT proven by this distant photo and no arrow is placed.
panels.creator: Sesamehoneytart
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

memory_rule: BIG = stout terminal exposed racemes; LITTLE = scattered short silk-tipped racemes along branches.
safety_note: 10 actual stored species JPEGs verified; 15 gallery panels include some EXTERNAL photos and DIFFERENT species comparisons. Several Harms images carry source-limited attributed educational permission, not Creative Commons. No new photos or microscopic arrows installed in this Lane 1 pass; 100% remains held.
field_rule: Trace the complete terminal flowering branches, corroborate with a real membranous collar/ligule and attached paired flowering units; do not certify by height, turkey-foot silhouette, or sheath color alone.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
